author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Mesoscale Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Phase Behavior, Interactome Architecture, and Cellular Function
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to organelle-scale structures with distinct material properties (liquid, gel, solid) that dictate cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects sequence-encoded molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material states and their functional/pathological consequences across the proteome. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize eight distinct public data ecosystems—(1) condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), (2) IDR and phase-separation propensity predictors (PScore, catGRANULE, FuzDrop), (3) genome-scale interactome and co-complex data (BioGRID, STRING, hu.MAP), (4) subcellular localization atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell live-imaging library), (5) structural data from cryo-EM/ET of cellular condensates (EMDB), (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived material-property measurements curated from literature, (7) disease mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-forming proteins, and (8) evolutionary conservation data (UniProt, Pfam) across species. By integrating these previously siloed resources, we will build a computational framework—the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas (CoMA)—that links sequence features to predicted material properties, interactome connectivity, and functional/disease outcomes at proteome scale. Specific aims include: (1) constructing a harmonized, machine-readable dataset unifying sequence, structural, biophysical, and phenotypic condensate data for >2,000 human proteins; (2) applying interpretable machine learning and network-based approaches to identify sequence and interaction motifs (the 'molecular grammar') that predict emergent material states and multiphase organization (e.g., core-shell condensates); (3) testing whether disease-associated mutations preferentially disrupt predicted grammar features linked to material-state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer; and (4) validating framework predictions against independent public datasets not used in model training. This task exceeds single-lab capacity: it requires biophysicists who understand phase-separation thermodynamics, structural biologists interpreting cryo-EM data, computational biologists building predictive models, cell biologists validating localization/functional data, and clinicians/geneticists linking findings to disease—expertise no single laboratory possesses. NCEMS support is essential to provide computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous, differently formatted datasets, to convene the necessary interdisciplinary expertise, and to establish shared open-science standards for reproducible mesoscale data synthesis. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis pipelines will be released as FAIR, versioned resources via GitHub and Zenodo, accompanied by interactive visualization tools for the broader community. The Working Group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computational biology, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning interpretability, and collaborative open-science workflows—directly cultivating the data-savvy, cross-disciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis effort promises to resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how simple sequence-encoded interactions give rise to complex, function-defining mesoscale organization, with direct implications for understanding proteinopathies and designing synthetic condensates.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Sequence Grammar to Cellular Phenotype: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Mesoscale Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Omics Synthesis of Phase Separation Determinants and Cellular Consequences
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level features (disordered sequences, multivalent interactions, post-translational modifications) give rise to organelle-scale material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn shape cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at each of these scales, the field lacks an integrated, predictive framework linking sequence-encoded biophysics to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists not from lack of data but from its fragmentation across incompatible domains: biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), disorder and sequence-feature repositories (MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold/ESMFold structural predictions), high-content and super-resolution imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting), single-cell and bulk multi-omics (expression stoichiometry, PTM databases like PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) documenting condensate-associated disease mutations. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, cell imaging analytics, and clinical genomics needed to unify these resources.

This Working Group will address the central question: What sequence-encoded biophysical grammar governs the emergent material properties of condensates, and how do perturbations to this grammar propagate to cellular and organismal phenotypes? We will pursue three synthesis aims. (1) Construct a harmonized cross-database resource linking condensate-forming proteins to quantitative sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, predicted secondary structure) using standardized ontologies, resolving inconsistent annotations across LLPS databases. (2) Train interpretable machine learning models that predict mesoscale material properties (viscosity class, multiphase organization, dynamic exchange rates) from these molecular features, validated against quantitative imaging datasets (FRAP recovery curves, condensate size/number distributions from HPA and OpenCell), enabling discovery of emergent 'grammar rules' not evident from single-protein studies. (3) Map disease-associated mutations (ClinVar, COSMIC) within condensate-relevant sequence regions onto predicted mesoscale property shifts, and cross-reference with single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data to identify cell-type-specific vulnerabilities where altered condensate stoichiometry may drive pathology (e.g., neurodegeneration, cancer).

This project intrinsically requires collaboration beyond any individual lab: biophysicists modeling polymer thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians curating disorder predictions, cell biologists interpreting high-content imaging phenotypes, and clinical genomicists linking variants to disease—together with data scientists capable of harmonizing heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets into a single predictive framework. NCEMS support is essential to convene this diverse team, provide computational infrastructure for large-scale data harmonization, and establish shared analytical standards. All curated datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows will be released as an open-access resource (GitHub/Zenodo, FAIR-compliant), including a web-based condensate property predictor for community use. The Working Group will embed graduate students and postdocs directly in cross-disciplinary sub-teams, pairing computational trainees with wet-lab-trained condensate biologists, providing structured mentorship in reproducible multi-omic synthesis and building a cohort of researchers fluent in both molecular biophysics and data science—directly advancing NCEMS's mission to train a data-savvy mesoscale biology workforce.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Mesoscale Condensate Emergence: A Cross-Database Synthesis Linking Sequence Features, Structural Organization, and Cellular Phenotype
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation and related self-organization processes—exemplify mesoscale emergence: simple molecular interactions between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to complex, functionally consequential structures that cannot be predicted from single-molecule properties alone. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensate-forming proteins (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro), disorder and sequence features (MobiDB, DisProt), protein-protein and protein-RNA interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, RNAct), subcellular imaging (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting, OpenCell), and emerging cryo-electron tomography maps of native cellular architecture (EMPIAR, CZ Imaging Institute datasets), no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features scale up to determine condensate material properties (viscosity, multiphasicity, exchange dynamics) and their downstream cellular consequences (transcriptional regulation, stress response, signaling compartmentalization). This gap persists because the requisite data are scattered across incompatible formats, curated by different scientific communities (biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and computational scientists), and require integration at a scale beyond any single laboratory's capacity.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team—including soft-matter biophysicists, structural/cryo-EM specialists, cell biologists studying condensate function, and machine-learning/data scientists—to build an integrated, open-access Mesoscale Condensate Atlas that harmonizes sequence-level features, empirically measured biophysical parameters (partition coefficients, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching rates, viscosity estimates), interactome connectivity, and high-resolution imaging/tomography data across human, yeast, and model organism datasets. Using this atlas, we will address three synthesis-driven questions: (1) What combinations of sequence grammar (charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, RNA-binding motifs) and interactome topology best predict condensate formation propensity and material state across proteomes? (2) Do condensates exhibit conserved scaling laws or percolation-like thresholds relating molecular valency/concentration to emergent material properties, and are these principles conserved across cell types and species? (3) Can integrated molecular-to-imaging data reveal generalizable ‘emergence signatures’—quantitative markers that predict when a condensate transitions from a passive assembly to one with regulatory or catalytic function at the cellular level?

We will develop novel network-based and generative AI models trained on this synthesized cross-scale dataset, producing publicly available, reproducible pipelines (via containerized workflows and FAIR-compliant repositories) that the community can extend to new proteins or organisms. This project requires NCEMS support because it demands sustained, coordinated data harmonization across incompatible legacy databases maintained by distinct research communities, computational infrastructure for large-scale multi-modal integration, and structured collaboration between biophysics and cell biology groups that rarely co-author work. The initiative will provide hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data science, biophysical modeling, and open-science practices, producing a new generation of scientists equipped to study emergence phenomena computationally. Ultimately, this work will establish generalizable principles governing how molecular-scale interactions generate mesoscale cellular architecture—a foundational advance for predictive cell biology.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Cross-Database Synthesis Linking Sequence Features, Structural Disorder, and Mesoscale Material Properties to Cellular Function
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) give rise to material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that cannot be predicted from single-molecule biophysics alone. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data—spanning sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB, disorder predictors like MobiDB), interactome data (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING), live-cell imaging datasets with FRAP/partition coefficients reported in hundreds of primary papers, and disease-variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC)—no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features generate emergent mesoscale properties and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because no single lab possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and cell biology, nor the bandwidth to curate and harmonize the fragmented, heterogeneous data across dozens of independent studies using inconsistent experimental conditions and metrics.

We propose a Working Group to build an integrated, machine-learning-ready meta-resource and mechanistic model connecting three data tiers: (1) molecular grammar (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs, stoichiometry from proteomics/interactome data), (2) mesoscale material properties (extracted via natural language processing and manual curation from published FRAP recovery curves, partition coefficients, and turbidity/phase diagrams), and (3) cellular/organismal outcomes (localization data from the Human Protein Atlas, disease-associated mutations, and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic correlates of condensate dysregulation in cancer and neurodegeneration cohorts). Using this harmonized dataset, we will develop interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating sequence, structure, and interaction features) to predict emergent condensate properties from molecular composition, and test whether specific 'grammar motifs' generalize across unrelated protein families and species—a question unanswerable without large-scale cross-dataset synthesis.

The project requires collaboration among biophysicists specializing in LLPS thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians, data scientists skilled in NLP-based literature mining, cell biologists with condensate imaging expertise, and clinical genomics researchers—expertise no single lab combines. NCEMS support is essential for data harmonization infrastructure, computational resources for large-scale model training, and coordination across geographically distributed teams. All curated datasets, ontologies for condensate property annotation, and trained models will be released as an open, FAIR-compliant resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with reproducible workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow), enabling community reuse. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams, receiving hands-on training in data harmonization, ML model development, and biophysical interpretation—directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology: how simple molecular rules generate the astonishing diversity of condensate behaviors and their roles in health and disease, while establishing a generalizable template for data-driven discovery of emergent properties in other mesoscale biological systems.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Multi-Modal Data Synthesis Across Sequence, Structure, Interactome, and Imaging Scales
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where local biomolecular interactions give rise to system-level properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that dictate cellular function in transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets, no unified framework connects the molecular determinants of phase behavior (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs, post-translational modifications) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences. This gap persists because relevant data are scattered across incompatible resources: sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), post-translational modification atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), protein abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and heterogeneous imaging/biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, and machine learning required to harmonize these disparate data types into a predictive, mechanistic framework.

This Working Group will assemble condensate biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and machine learning experts to build an integrated, open-access resource—the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA)—that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale phase behavior and cellular outcomes. We will: (1) curate and cross-reference sequence-based determinants (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic sticker density) with experimentally reported condensate material properties (liquid, gel, solid; FRAP-derived mobile fractions; concentration-dependent phase boundaries); (2) integrate interactome and stoichiometry data to model condensates as emergent network phenomena, testing whether percolation-like thresholds in interaction valency predict phase transition points; (3) incorporate PTM and cellular context data (abundance, localization, cell-type specificity) to explain condition-dependent condensate emergence versus dissolution; and (4) apply supervised and unsupervised machine learning to identify generalizable 'rules' distinguishing functional condensates from aberrant aggregates linked to disease (e.g., neurodegeneration-associated solidification).

A central scientific question we will address: Can mesoscale material properties of condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do emergent properties require irreducible knowledge of cellular context (concentration, crowding, PTM state)? Answering this tests fundamental assumptions about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology.

This project is infeasible for any single lab given the scale of cross-database harmonization, the breadth of required expertise, and the need for standardized ontologies bridging biophysics and cell biology communities. NCEMS support will fund coordinated data-wrangling sprints, shared computational infrastructure, and workshops to establish community standards for condensate data annotation. All curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, and predictive models will be released under FAIR principles via a public repository and interactive web tool. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning—directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will yield a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale emergent properties from molecular data, with broad applicability beyond condensates to other emergent cellular phenomena.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Sequence to Cellular Phenotype: A Multi-Database Synthesis of the Molecular Grammar Governing Emergent Material Properties of Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to system-level material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) that in turn dictate cellular outcomes such as transcriptional regulation, stress adaptation, and disease pathology. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data, the field remains fragmented: sequence-feature databases (MobiDB, D2P2), curated LLPS protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, PhaSePro, DrLLPS), single-cell condensate imaging repositories (CD-CODE, Human Protein Atlas subcellular data), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), and disease-mutation resources (ClinVar, COSMIG, gnomAD) exist as disconnected silos, each captured by different labs using incompatible vocabularies, scales, and experimental readouts. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, network science, and clinical genomics needed to integrate these resources into a predictive, mechanistic framework linking molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotype. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—biophysicists studying condensate material properties, computational structural biologists, network biologists, cell imaging specialists, and clinical genomicists—to build the first cross-scale, harmonized data resource and predictive model connecting (1) sequence-encoded molecular features (IDR composition, stickers-and-spacers architecture, post-translational modification sites, RNA-binding motifs), (2) network-level context (interactome connectivity, co-condensation partners, stoichiometry), (3) empirically measured mesoscale material properties (FRAP-derived mobility, viscosity, multiphase demixing, aging/hardening propensity compiled from published biophysical studies), and (4) higher-order cellular and organismal outcomes (subcellular localization patterns, stress-responsive condensate remodeling, and disease-associated mutations affecting phase behavior). Using graph-based machine learning and multi-modal data fusion, we will construct a genome-wide predictive atlas of condensate-forming proteins that infers emergent material properties for thousands of uncharacterized proteins, tests whether specific sequence-network signatures predict multiphase organization or aberrant hardening linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic mutations, and identifies general design principles by which molecular-scale interactions propagate to cellular-scale function. Model predictions will be rigorously validated against independent, held-out public datasets (orthogonal imaging studies, biophysical measurements not used in training) to ensure generalizability rather than dataset-specific overfitting. All harmonized datasets, ontology mappings, code, and trained models will be released as an open, versioned community resource (via NCEMS-supported infrastructure) to enable reuse and extension by the broader condensate biology community. The working group will embed graduate students and postdocs in cross-lab data harmonization, biophysical modeling, and network-based machine learning, providing hands-on training in reproducible, large-scale synthesis science. By resolving inconsistencies across independently generated datasets and establishing shared standards for describing condensate material properties, this project will produce mechanistic insight into why and how mesoscale emergence arises from molecular interactions—addressing a fundamental, long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology that is intractable without cross-institutional, cross-disciplinary data synthesis at NCEMS scale.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Sequence Grammar to Cellular Phenotype: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence and Its Disruption in Disease
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from weak multivalent interactions among biomolecules to produce compartments with system-level functions (e.g., stress granules, transcriptional hubs, nucleoli) that cannot be predicted from single-protein properties alone. Despite an explosion of public data describing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, subcellular localization, and disease-associated mutations, no integrated framework exists linking molecular sequence features to network-level organization to cellular phenotype. This gap persists because the relevant expertise—biophysics of disordered proteins, network science, cell imaging informatics, and clinical genetics—is distributed across disparate communities that rarely collaborate, and because no single lab possesses the computational infrastructure or cross-domain fluency to harmonize these heterogeneous data types at scale.

This Working Group will synthesize five major public resources: (1) sequence-based condensate databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS) and IDR predictors (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) proteome-wide interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct); (3) high-resolution subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, CellPainting); (4) structural and AlphaFold-derived conformational ensembles for disordered/multivalent proteins; and (5) disease-mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-associated proteins. Our central hypothesis is that emergent condensate behavior is governed by a decodable 'grammar' spanning three scales: (a) molecular grammar—sticker-spacer patterning, charge blockiness, and aromatic density within IDRs; (b) network grammar—topological features of interaction hubs (multivalency, promiscuity, community structure) that nucleate condensation; and (c) phenotypic grammar—how these features manifest as condensate size, dynamics, and localization observable in imaging data, and how their disruption by disease mutations produces pathological aggregation or loss-of-function.

The team will integrate machine learning (graph neural networks trained on PPI topology plus sequence embeddings), coarse-grained biophysical simulation benchmarking, and image-derived phenotypic quantification to build predictive models that generalize across protein families and cell types—an analysis impossible without cross-disciplinary data fusion at this scale. Deliverables include: a unified, versioned 'Condensate Emergence Atlas' linking sequence, network, and phenotype data with open APIs; predictive models identifying condensate-prone proteins and mutation-driven emergent dysfunction relevant to neurodegeneration and cancer; and a reproducible open-source pipeline (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized) for community reuse. The Working Group will comprise biophysicists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomics researchers from institutions varying in size and geography, explicitly recruiting early-career co-PIs and including graduate students/postdocs in every workflow layer, with structured training in reproducible multi-omic synthesis, FAIR data practices, and interdisciplinary communication. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be deposited on public repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Synapse) under NCEMS open science guidelines, enabling the broader community to test, extend, and apply this cross-scale framework to other emergent mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Cross-Scale Data Synthesis of Sequence, Structure, and Material Properties
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: collective material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, aging into gels or solids) arise from thousands of transient, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs). Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding of how molecular 'grammar' dictates emergent mesoscale behavior remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, EMPIAR), proteomic and interactome studies of condensate composition (BioGRID, IntAct, RNAct), biophysical measurements of material properties (FRAP recovery rates, viscosity, surface tension) buried in supplementary tables of hundreds of papers, and PTM/disease-variant databases (PhosphoSitePlus, ClinVar) linking condensate dysregulation to pathology. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to harmonize these heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets—spanning atomic structure to cellular phenotype—into a unified predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and data scientists to construct a curated, interoperable meta-database and companion machine-learning framework—CondensateAtlas—that integrates sequence features (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs), structural/ultrastructural data (condensate size, shape, multiphase organization from imaging archives), interactome-derived compositional networks, and quantitative material-property measurements curated via natural-language-processing-assisted literature mining and manual expert curation. Using this integrated resource, we will (1) test whether sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features quantitatively predict emergent viscoelastic properties across condensate types, (2) identify structural and compositional signatures that distinguish functional liquid-like condensates from pathological solid-like aggregates linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic variants, and (3) develop generalizable biophysical/ML models capable of predicting mesoscale material behavior from primary sequence and cellular context, tested against held-out experimental datasets. Statistical and generative modeling approaches (Gaussian process regression, graph neural networks trained on interaction networks, physics-informed biophysical polymer models) will be co-developed by computational and wet-lab collaborators to ensure biological interpretability.

This project requires NCEMS support because it depends on cross-institutional data harmonization, standardized ontology development for condensate properties, and computational infrastructure beyond any single lab's capacity, while uniting communities (structural biology, soft-matter physics, cell biology, genomics) that rarely interact directly. The working group will include early-career researchers and trainees who will lead specific data curation and modeling modules, receiving hands-on training in FAIR data practices, reproducible workflow design (Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines), and multidisciplinary team science. All curated datasets, ontologies, trained models, and analysis code will be released as open-access community resources via Zenodo/GitHub, with a living database designed for continuous community contribution. By synthesizing molecular-to-mesoscale data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle—how simple molecular rules generate complex emergent condensate behavior—while generating a foundational, reusable resource for the mesoscale biology community.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Condensatome: A Multiscale Data Synthesis Framework Linking Molecular Grammar to Emergent Biomolecular Condensate Function
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membrane-less assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: they arise from collective, multivalent interactions among proteins and nucleic acids, yet exhibit properties (viscosity, selective permeability, catalytic enhancement, signaling thresholds) not predictable from any single component.
