This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across disconnected resources—intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predictors (MobiDB, IUPred), condensate component databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE), structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell), single-cell/spatial transcriptomics, and disease-variant catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC). Synthesizing these heterogeneous, multiscale datasets requires expertise spanning biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational modeling, evolutionary biology, and clinical genetics—expertise no single lab possesses, and integration efforts that exceed what any two-lab collaboration could reasonably undertake.

This Working Group will construct an open, queryable 'Condensatome' resource and analytical framework that integrates these disparate datasets to answer a fundamental question: What generalizable molecular features—sequence composition, IDR architecture, multivalent interaction motifs, post-translational modification sites, and structural flexibility—predict the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates (nucleation propensity, material state, compositional selectivity, functional output), and how do disease-associated mutations perturb these emergent properties to drive pathology?

Our approach proceeds in three synthesis phases. First, we will harmonize condensate component annotations, interaction networks, and structural/disorder predictions into a unified schema, applying network-based and machine-learning methods (graph neural networks, multivalency scoring) to identify molecular 'grammars' associated with distinct condensate material states and functions. Second, we will cross-reference these molecular grammars with imaging-derived phenotypic data (condensate size, number, dynamics from public live-cell datasets) and single-cell expression contexts to model how cellular environment (concentration, crowding, post-translational state) modulates emergent phase behavior across cell types. Third, we will overlay disease-variant data to test whether mutations disrupting predicted phase-separation grammar correlate with aberrant condensate formation implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-granule pathologies, generating testable hypotheses for the broader community.

The Working Group will assemble investigators across career stages and institution types—biophysicists modeling phase behavior, structural biologists curating disorder/structure data, cell biologists with imaging expertise, computational scientists building integrative ML pipelines, and clinical geneticists connecting variants to disease—reflecting the transdisciplinary scope NCEMS uniquely enables. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis workflows will be released as open, versioned, reproducible pipelines (via GitHub/Zenodo) accompanied by tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on data harmonization and modeling subprojects, receiving structured training in FAIR data practices, cross-disciplinary communication, and reproducible computational biology, directly building the data-savvy workforce this call seeks to cultivate while resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Cross-Scale Synthesis of Sequence, Network, Structural, and Imaging Data
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (material state, composition, exchange dynamics) arise from combinatorial molecular interactions and cannot be predicted from any single molecule or interaction alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based predictors of disorder and multivalency, curated condensate composition databases, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks, structural ensemble data, single-molecule dynamics measurements, and cellular phenotype datasets have been generated by disconnected communities using incompatible vocabularies and formats. No integrated framework currently links molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and its downstream cellular consequences. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public resources into a unified, predictive, and mechanistic framework for condensate emergence. We will integrate: (1) sequence-derived features of intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, and multivalent motifs from UniProt, MobiDB, and IDRome conformational ensemble data; (2) curated condensate composition and phase-behavior annotations from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE; (3) protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction topology from BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct; (4) structural context from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and PDB; (5) subcellular localization and condensate imaging data from the Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer; (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived exchange kinetics extracted from published literature and condensate databases; and (7) disease-associated variant data from ClinVar and COSMIC. Using this multi-modal resource, we will address three central questions: First, what combinations of sequence, network topology, and structural features best predict whether a protein participates in condensate formation, and do these features generalize across condensate types (stress granules, transcriptional condensates, nucleoli)? Second, does interactome topology (e.g., hub connectivity, clustering coefficients) correlate with emergent material properties such as liquid-to-solid transitions and exchange dynamics measured by FRAP? Third, can disease-associated mutations be systematically mapped onto this framework to identify variants that specifically perturb condensate emergence, and do such perturbations correlate with altered transcriptional noise or cellular phenotypes documented in single-cell RNA-seq datasets (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas)? This synthesis requires computational infrastructure and cross-disciplinary expertise—spanning biophysical theory, network science, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics—that no single lab possesses, and it demands harmonization of heterogeneous, differently-curated public databases at a scale only achievable through coordinated collaboration. Deliverables include an open-access, version-controlled integrated database and machine-learning framework (CondensateAtlas), reproducible analysis pipelines, and a predictive model relating molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale phenotype. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in biophysical modeling, network analysis, and open, reproducible data science, directly building the data-savvy interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Emergent Condensate Material Properties: A Multi-Database Synthesis Linking Sequence, Structure, and Cellular Function
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: their material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, component exchange dynamics) arise from collective interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications, yet these properties cannot be predicted from single-molecule features alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), condensate-specific proteomic and interactome maps (CD-CODE, BioGRID, IntAct), structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-content imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting), and functional perturbation screens (CRISPR-based condensate disruption studies, disease-mutation databases like ClinVar and COSMIC). No integrated framework currently connects molecular grammar to emergent material properties to downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell imaging, and machine learning—to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and predictive modeling framework addressing a fundamental question: What combinatorial rules of sequence composition, structural motifs, PTMs, and interaction networks give rise to specific emergent material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally determine cellular outcomes such as transcriptional bursting, stress granule dynamics, and signaling fidelity? 

The working group will first construct a harmonized meta-database linking condensate-resident proteins across sequence/structural feature sets, experimentally measured or imaging-inferred material properties (FRAP recovery rates, droplet fusion kinetics, aspect ratios extracted from public microscopy datasets), and interactome/expression context. Using this resource, we will train interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating AlphaFold-derived structural embeddings and disorder/PTM annotations) to predict emergent material properties from molecular features, explicitly testing whether scaling laws or phase diagrams generalize across protein families and cellular contexts. Second, we will cross-reference predicted material-property phenotypes with functional perturbation datasets (e.g., condensate-disrupting mutations linked to disease, optogenetic clustering screens) to test causal links between mesoscale material state and higher-order cellular function, addressing long-standing puzzles such as why chemically similar condensates (e.g., stress granules vs. P-bodies) exhibit distinct dynamics and functional consequences. 

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging analysis, and cell biology, plus computational infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets. NCEMS support will enable dataset harmonization workshops, shared computational pipelines, and coordination across geographically distributed labs. All curated datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned community resource (FAIR-compliant), with tutorials and hackathon-style training events specifically designed to onboard graduate students and postdocs into data-intensive condensate biology, cultivating a new generation of researchers fluent in both wet-lab condensate biophysics and computational data synthesis.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Phenotype Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis Initiative
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic mesoscale emergent phenomenon, arising from multivalent, low-affinity interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct biophysical properties and cellular functions. Despite an explosion of data characterizing condensates across scales—from intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence features to interactome networks to live-cell imaging phenotypes—the field lacks an integrated framework connecting molecular grammar to cellular outcome. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize disparate, publicly available datasets spanning five layers of biological organization: (1) sequence/structural databases of phase-separating proteins (PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CatGRANULE outputs); (2) proteome-wide interactome and post-translational modification data (BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, STRING); (3) cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, CZI Imaging Data Resource); (4) single-molecule and FRAP kinetic measurements of condensate dynamics deposited in supplementary datasets across hundreds of published studies; and (5) single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data linking condensate-associated protein expression to cellular phenotypes and disease states (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, CCLE). No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, biophysical expertise, and cell biology domain knowledge required to harmonize these heterogeneous, non-standardized datasets—many collected with different assay conditions, buffer compositions, and imaging modalities—into a unified predictive model. This is precisely the kind of large-scale, cross-disciplinary synthesis challenge NCEMS is positioned to catalyze. Our working group will bring together biophysicists specializing in polymer theory of LLPS, structural biologists with cryo-EM/ET expertise, computational biologists skilled in graph-based interactome analysis, and cell biologists studying condensate function in stress response, transcription, and neurodegeneration. We will develop a standardized ontology and data harmonization pipeline (leveraging FAIR principles) to align sequence features, biophysical parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, surface tension), and phenotypic readouts into a unified multi-scale database. Using this integrated resource, we will apply machine learning and biophysical modeling to test three novel hypotheses: (i) whether condensate material properties (liquid vs. gel vs. solid) can be predicted from combinatorial sequence grammar and interactor stoichiometry; (ii) whether condensate emergence thresholds correlate with disease-associated mutations across cancer and neurodegeneration datasets; and (iii) whether evolutionary conservation patterns in IDRs predict condensate functional conservation across species. Deliverables include an open-access, versioned meta-database (deposited via Zenodo/GitHub with full analytical code), a generalizable predictive model of condensate emergence, and reproducible workflows adhering to community open-science standards. The project will directly train 4-6 graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, biophysical modeling, and open science practices through structured hackathons and co-mentorship across participating labs. By synthesizing molecular-scale sequence data with cellular-scale phenotypic outcomes, this working group will resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how simple sequence and interaction rules generate the emergent complexity of condensate behavior—while establishing a template for future mesoscale synthesis research supported by NCEMS.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Emergent Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis Framework Linking Sequence, Structure, and Cellular Phenotype
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), RNA, and multivalent interactions generate organelle-like structures with functions not predictable from individual molecular components alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, structural biology datasets, single-cell spatial atlases, and functional genomic screens exist in isolation, preventing a unified understanding of how molecular grammar dictates emergent mesoscale organization and downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning—to integrate five classes of publicly available data: (1) curated LLPS driver/scaffold databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepPro) and disorder annotations (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) structural and interaction data from the PDB, EMDB, and AlphaFold/ESMFold predicted structures, including cryo-ET tomograms of native condensates; (3) single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, HuBMAP, Tabula Sapiens) capturing condensate-associated protein expression across cell states; (4) high-throughput perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq, genome-wide CRISPR screens, ORFeome overexpression libraries) linking condensate-associated genes to cellular phenotypes; and (5) live-cell imaging repositories (e.g., OpenCell, LLPSDB) documenting condensate dynamics, material properties, and stress responses. No single dataset or lab possesses the breadth needed to bridge molecular sequence features to emergent mesoscale phase behavior and its physiological consequences—this synthesis requires simultaneous fluency in biophysical polymer theory, structural bioinformatics, single-cell genomics, and network-based phenotype mapping. Our central hypothesis is that a generalizable 'molecular grammar'—combinations of valency, disorder patterning, post-translational modification sites, and RNA-binding motifs—predicts not only condensate formation propensity but also material state transitions (liquid-to-gel-to-solid) that underlie both normal cellular function and disease-associated aggregation. We will develop multi-modal graph neural network models trained on integrated sequence-structure-interaction data, validated against independent perturbation and imaging datasets, to predict emergent condensate properties and their causal links to cellular outcomes such as stress granule dynamics, transcriptional condensate function, and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation. The working group will produce: (i) an open, harmonized multi-omic condensate database with standardized ontologies, (ii) predictive models and interactive tools for the community, and (iii) a mechanistic framework connecting molecular-scale grammar to mesoscale emergence and cellular phenotype. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be released under FAIR and open-science principles via community repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase). The project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, reproducible computational workflows, and collaborative team science, directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how simple molecular rules give rise to complex, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in living cells.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Cross-Species, Multi-Omics Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence and Its Cellular Consequences
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation and related processes—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to functional subcellular compartments not predictable from any single molecule's properties. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive 'grammar' linking molecular-scale features (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalency, stoichiometry, post-translational modification patterns) to mesoscale material properties (droplet viscosity, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes (stress granule dynamics, transcriptional bursting, cell fate transitions). This gap persists because the necessary data are scattered across incompatible resources curated by disconnected communities: biophysicists studying in vitro phase diagrams, cell biologists generating high-content imaging atlases, proteomicists cataloging condensate constituents, evolutionary biologists tracking IDR conservation, and clinical genomicists annotating disease-associated mutations. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these disparate data types into a coherent cross-scale model. This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, computational structural biologists, cell imaging specialists, evolutionary genomicists, and clinical variant scientists to synthesize existing public datasets—including PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB (condensate composition and phase behavior), OpenCell and the Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization imaging), BioGRID/IntAct (interactomes), Human Cell Atlas and single-cell perturbation atlases (transcriptomic consequences across cell states), OrthoDB/Ensembl (cross-species IDR conservation), and ClinVar/COSMIC/gnomAD (disease-linked mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Using this integrated dataset, we will: (1) train interpretable machine learning models that map sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features to empirically observed condensate material states and client recruitment specificity; (2) test whether evolutionary conservation patterns of IDR grammar predict functional robustness or tunability of condensate properties across orthologous proteins in diverse species; (3) determine whether disease-associated mutations in condensate scaffolds and clients cluster at predicted grammar 'hotspots' and whether this predicts pathological mesoscale-to-cellular phenotypic outcomes (e.g., aberrant stress granule persistence in neurodegeneration, altered chromatin condensate formation in cancer); and (4) build a generalizable cross-scale predictive framework linking molecular grammar to emergent cellular behavior, tested against independent public single-cell perturbation datasets. This synthesis is intractable for any individual lab given the scale of data harmonization, cross-domain expertise, and computational infrastructure required, and directly requires NCEMS support for data engineering, workshop convening, and shared analytical infrastructure. The Working Group will operate under FAIR and open-science principles, releasing all harmonized datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows via public repositories. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on each data-integration module, receiving structured training in multi-omics data science, biophysical modeling, and collaborative team science, while a rotating visiting-scholar program will recruit early-career researchers from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions to broaden participation. The project's central deliverable—a public, cross-species 'condensate grammar atlas'—will provide the field's first quantitative bridge between molecular sequence, mesoscale organization, and cellular emergent behavior.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Mesoscale Emergence: A Cross-Database Synthesis Linking Biomolecular Condensate Sequence Features to Material States and Cellular Phenotypes
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon in which collective molecular interactions give rise to emergent material properties (liquid, gel, solid, multiphase architectures) that are not predictable from any single constituent protein or RNA. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, proteomic condensate composition datasets, cryo-electron tomography structural data, live-cell imaging archives, disease mutation catalogs, and functional genomics screens are housed in disconnected repositories, analyzed with incompatible metrics, and rarely cross-validated against one another. No individual laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, computational sequence analysis, cell imaging, evolutionary genomics, and clinical genetics needed to integrate these resources into a unified predictive framework. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize eight major public data classes—LLPSDB and PhaSepDB (experimentally curated phase-separating proteins and conditions), CD-CODE (condensate composition and localization), MobiDB/DisProt (intrinsically disordered region annotations), EMDB cryo-electron tomograms of native condensates, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular imaging, ClinVar/COSMIC disease variants mapped onto disordered regions, multi-species sequence conservation (OrthoDB, UCSC multiz alignments), and DepMap/BioGRID-ORCS functional perturbation screens—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Our central scientific question is: what molecular grammar (sequence patterning of stickers, spacers, charge blocks, and short linear motifs) determines the emergent mesoscale material state and multiphase organization of condensates, and how do these physical properties causally propagate to organelle-level morphology and cell-scale phenotypes, including their disruption in disease? We will apply stickers-and-spacers biophysical theory and modern sequence-to-function machine learning models, trained on the harmonized dataset, to predict material state and client selectivity directly from primary sequence, then validate predictions against orthogonal image-derived morphological signatures (condensate number, size, sphericity, coalescence dynamics) extracted computationally from public imaging archives. We will further test whether disease-associated mutations preferentially alter predicted material properties rather than simple phase separation propensity, and whether evolutionary conservation patterns track functionally important mesoscale properties rather than sequence identity alone. This effort demands NCEMS-scale infrastructure: standardized ontologies for condensate material properties, automated cross-database entity resolution (protein identifiers, cell lines, imaging conditions), and computational pipelines for large-scale image feature extraction—capabilities beyond any single lab or existing bilateral collaboration. The team will unite condensate biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational/AI researchers, evolutionary biologists, and clinical geneticists across institutions varying in size and geography. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across all analytical stages, receiving hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, biophysical modeling, and open-science workflows. All harmonized datasets, trained models, analysis code, and condensate material-property ontologies will be released under FAIR principles via public repositories, providing a durable community resource for predicting and interpreting mesoscale emergence in cell biology and disease.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis from Sequence to Cellular Phenotype
abstract: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications give rise to macroscopic material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn drive cellular functions such as transcriptional control, stress response, and signal transduction. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across biophysics, structural biology, proteomics, and cell imaging, the field lacks a unified framework connecting molecular-scale determinants to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular/disease phenotypes. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize disparate public datasets—including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE (condensate composition and in vitro phase behavior), AlphaFold DB and PDB (structural/disorder predictions), Human Protein Atlas and Human Cell Atlas (expression, subcellular localization, single-cell heterogeneity), BioGRID/STRING (interactomes), and ClinVar/COSMIC (disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—to build a predictive, cross-scale model of condensate emergence. Our central question: Can molecular-level features (sequence grammar, valency, PTM sites, structural disorder) combined with cellular context (expression stoichiometry, localization, network connectivity) predict which proteins form condensates, the material properties of those condensates, and their functional or pathological consequences when perturbed by disease mutations? This question cannot be addressed by any single lab, as it requires integrating fundamentally different data modalities—biophysical phase diagrams, structural predictions, single-cell transcriptomics/proteomics, network biology, and clinical genomics—each requiring distinct domain expertise (biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists). The Working Group will develop harmonized ontologies and standardized feature representations across these datasets, construct machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating interactome topology and sequence-based transformers for disorder/valency prediction) to predict condensate propensity and material state, and validate predictions against orthogonal public datasets (e.g., proteome-wide condensate screens, stress granule proteomics). A key innovation is testing whether emergent condensate properties can be predicted purely from public data integration without new wet-lab experiments, and whether disease mutations disrupt predicted phase behavior in ways that explain pathological phenotypes (e.g., ALS-associated FUS/TDP-43 mutations). The team will include biophysicists (LLPS theory), structural biologists (AlphaFold-based feature engineering), computational/systems biologists (network and ML integration), cell biologists (phenotypic validation using public imaging), and clinical genomics experts (mutation-disease linkage), spanning multiple career stages and institutions. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams, receiving training in multi-omics data integration, reproducible computational pipelines, and biophysical modeling. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with a FAIR-compliant condensate feature database, enabling the broader community to test hypotheses about mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. This work directly advances NCEMS's mission by using purely existing data to resolve a fundamental puzzle in emergent cellular organization, requiring collaboration far beyond individual lab capacity, and producing durable, reusable synthesis resources for the field.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Mesoscale Emergence: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Formation, Material Properties, and Cellular Phenotype
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where collective molecular interactions produce organelle-like structures with properties (viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability) not predictable from any single protein's biochemistry. Despite thousands of published studies characterizing individual condensates, the field lacks a unified, cross-scale understanding of which sequence features, structural motifs, and interaction network topologies causally determine condensate material properties and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists because relevant data are fragmented across incompatible resources: intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence databases (e.g., DisProt, MobiDB), condensate proteome catalogs (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), protein-protein interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING), structural data from cryo-EM/cryo-ET and AlphaFold, quantitative live-cell imaging datasets (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, condensate size/number distributions from the Cell Image Library and BioImage Archive), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic datasets capturing phenotypic consequences of condensate dysregulation in disease contexts (ALS, cancer). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, network science, computer vision, and systems biology needed to integrate these disparate data modalities into a predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team—computational biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, network biologists, and machine learning experts—to synthesize existing public datasets into an integrated, multi-scale atlas linking molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotype. Specific aims include: (1) Curate and harmonize condensate proteomic, sequence, and structural datasets into a standardized ontology capturing IDR composition, multivalency, post-translational modification sites, and predicted AlphaFold conformational ensembles; (2) Develop machine learning models trained on quantitative imaging-derived material property measurements (droplet fusion rates, FRAP recovery kinetics, aspect ratios) to identify sequence/network features predictive of condensate viscoelasticity and stability across previously siloed studies; (3) Integrate condensate composition data with protein interaction networks and single-cell omics to test whether network centrality and connectivity of condensate-resident proteins predict cellular sensitivity to condensate perturbation (e.g., in stress granule dynamics during disease); (4) Build a publicly accessible, version-controlled computational pipeline and interactive database (following FAIR principles) enabling the community to query molecular determinants of mesoscale emergence across cell types and organisms.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it demands reconciling incompatible data formats, resolving conflicting condensate classification schemes across independent labs, and computational infrastructure for cross-referencing structural, network, and imaging data at scale—tasks infeasible for any individual collaboration. The working group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computer science, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, FAIR data stewardship, and emergence-focused hypothesis generation. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open-source resource, establishing a reusable framework for mesoscale emergence research applicable beyond condensate biology to other multi-scale cellular phenomena.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Cross-Database Synthesis Linking Sequence Features, Mesoscale Material Properties, and Cellular Phenotypes
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related processes—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular processes such as transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based predictors of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent motifs (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PLAAC, catGRANULE outputs), curated condensate composition and localization databases (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), high-content imaging repositories capturing condensate morphology and dynamics (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Cell Explorer), interactome and PTM databases (BioGRID, STRING, PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) linking condensate-associated mutations to disease. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these heterogeneous, multi-scale datasets into a unified predictive framework. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists to synthesize these public resources and address a fundamental question: what molecular-level 'grammar'—sequence composition, valency, PTM patterning, and stoichiometry—determines the emergent mesoscale material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally propagate to higher-order cellular phenotypes and disease states?

Our approach will proceed in three integrated phases. First, we will construct a harmonized, ontology-linked meta-database that cross-references sequence/structural features of condensate-forming proteins with experimentally reported material properties (extracted via text-mining and manual curation from published biophysical assays) and cellular imaging phenotypes. Second, we will apply machine learning and biophysical polymer models to identify generalizable sequence-to-material-property relationships, testing whether emergent condensate behaviors (e.g., liquid-to-gel transitions, multiphase architecture) can be predicted purely from primary sequence and interactome context, independent of any single protein family. Third, we will link these mesoscale signatures to organismal and disease-relevant outcomes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic stress-response datasets (GEO, Human Cell Atlas) and disease variant databases, testing whether condensate-destabilizing mutations converge on shared material-property signatures across neurodegenerative and cancer-associated proteins.

This project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: it requires no new experiments, relies entirely on integration of existing public datasets across previously unlinked disciplines, and demands collaborative infrastructure beyond any individual lab's capacity, including standardized data harmonization pipelines, shared computational resources, and cross-domain expertise. All curated datasets, ontologies, and analysis code will be released as open-source, FAIR-compliant resources through NCEMS infrastructure, accompanied by a public database and interactive visualization tool for the condensate research community. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across sub-teams (data curation, ML modeling, biophysical validation, phenotype integration), receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and open data science practices, directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce central to NCEMS's mission while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how molecular-scale interactions generate emergent, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in cells.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Sequence Grammar to Cellular Phenotype: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Data to Decode Rules of Mesoscale Emergence
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (viscosity, selective permeability, reaction enhancement) arise from ensembles of weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, and RNA. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at multiple scales—proteomic composition (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), sequence/disorder features (DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt), high-throughput in vitro phase diagrams, super-resolution and live-cell imaging (Cell Image Library, IDR/BioImage Archive), disease variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas)—these resources remain siloed within disciplinary boundaries (biophysics, structural biology, cell imaging, genetics, computational biology). No integrated framework currently links molecular-grammar features of condensate-forming proteins to their higher-order mesoscale material properties and ultimate cellular/phenotypic consequences, including disease-associated dysregulation.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and analytical framework: the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA). Our central scientific question is: What sequence-encoded and network-level features predict the emergent material and functional properties of condensates across scales, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this sequence-to-phenotype mapping? We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Integrate sequence/disorder databases with biophysical phase-behavior datasets to derive quantitative 'condensate grammars'—stoichiometric and compositional rules linking IDR patterning, charge blockiness, and multivalency to phase diagram parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity); (2) Cross-reference these molecular grammars with public imaging datasets to test whether in vitro biophysical predictors explain observed in-cell condensate morphology, dynamics, and localization across cell types; (3) Map disease-associated variants (ALS, FTD, cancer) onto condensate-forming proteins to determine whether mutations systematically shift emergent mesoscale properties in ways that correlate with pathological cellular phenotypes from public multi-omic disease datasets.

This project is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics/phase-separation theory, machine learning on heterogeneous imaging/sequence data, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics, plus harmonization of incompatible data formats and scales across at least six major public repositories. NCEMS support will fund a coordinated data harmonization pipeline, shared computational infrastructure, and recurring cross-disciplinary working sessions to reconcile conflicting metrics of 'phase separation propensity' across source databases. All harmonized datasets, predictive models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with FAIR metadata standards, accompanied by interactive tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, co-developing cross-training modules in biophysics, imaging analytics, and genomics, and co-authoring resulting publications and open-source software—directly cultivating a new generation of data-savvy researchers equipped to study emergence phenomena at the mesoscale.

author: claude-sonnet-5
title: From Molecular Grammar to Mesoscale Material Properties: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: the collective behavior of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) gives rise to structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that are not predictable from any single molecular feature alone. title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis from Sequence to Cellular Phenotype
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce organelle-like structures with distinct biochemical and mechanical properties. This Working Group proposes to synthesize five previously siloed classes of public data: (1) sequence-based IDR and low-complexity domain predictions (e.g., from MobiDB, PONDR-derived datasets); (2) curated condensate/LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro) cataloguing experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their in vitro conditions; (3) genome-scale PPI and co-expression networks (BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeHD); (4) quantitative single-cell imaging and localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas subcellular imaging, LLPSDB-linked microscopy) capturing condensate morphology, number, and dynamics; and (5) proteomic abundance and post-translational modification datasets (PhosphoSitePlus, PaxDb) that modulate condensation propensity in vivo. By harmonizing these disparate data types—spanning sequence, network, image, and abundance modalities—we will build predictive, mechanistic models of condensate emergence that no single dataset or disciplinary approach could achieve alone.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate emergence is governed by a combinatorial 'molecular grammar' operating simultaneously at three scales: intra-protein (IDR patterning, valency of interaction motifs), inter-protein (network connectivity, co-condensation partners), and cellular (local concentration, PTM state, compartment identity). Validation will leverage held-out experimental datasets and cross-species comparisons (yeast, human, plant) to test universality of discovered rules.

This project requires collaboration among condensate biophysicists, network biologists, imaging data scientists, and machine learning experts—expertise no single lab possesses collectively—and NCEMS support for compute infrastructure, data harmonization workshops, and cross-database ontology alignment. By transforming fragmented public data into a unified framework, this project will advance a mechanistic understanding of how molecular interactions generate emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular behavior.

title: Predicting Emergent RNP Condensate Assembly and Cell-State Consequences from Public Multi-Omic and Imaging Data
abstract: Membraneless ribonucleoprotein condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, and nuclear speckles are archetypal mesoscale systems: they emerge from many weak molecular interactions yet shape translation, RNA fate, signaling, and cell survival. The goal is not simply to classify condensate components, but to identify generalizable rules explaining how emergent mesoscale properties arise from molecular composition and how these properties influence higher-order cell states such as translational arrest, antiviral response, proteostasis failure, and stress adaptation. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can assemble the needed expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, quantitative imaging, biophysics, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure, nor can it coordinate the community standards required to make heterogeneous public data interoperable.
